title: Lab 3: Linear Regression — Model Specification, Comparison, and Interpretation
text:
Introduction
This report investigates factors associated with employee ratings of their workplace. I will estimate and compare competing linear regression models, evaluate model diagnostics, and interpret the results of a preferred model.

title: Lab 3: Linear Regression — Model Specification, Comparison, and Interpretation
text:
Data

data("attitude", package = "datasets")

analysis_data <- attitude |>
  dplyr::select(rating, complaints, learning, raises)

The analysis uses the built-in R dataset attitude. The analysis dataset has 30 departments and four variables: overall workplace rating (rating), handling of employee complaints (complaints), opportunity to learn (learning), and raises based on performance (raises). The scores represent department-level percentages of favourable employee responses. So, each observation represents a department instead of an individual employee.

  summarise(
    Mean = mean(Score),
    SD = sd(Score),
    Minimum = min(Score),
    Maximum = max(Score),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

descriptive_stats |>

    title = "Descriptive Statistics",

Distribution of workplace ratings

ggplot(analysis_data, aes(x = rating)) +
  geom_histogram(
    aes(y = after_stat(density)),
    bins = 8,
    fill = "lightblue",
    color = "white"

  geom_density(
    color = "navy",
    linewidth = 1
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Overall Workplace Ratings",
    x = "Overall workplace rating",
    y = "Density"
  ) +

Distribution of overall workplace ratings across 30 departments.






Relationships between ratings and predictors

Overall workplace rating and raises based on performance.






Summary of exploratory findings
Overall workplace ratings averaged 64.63 (SD = 12.17), ranging from 40 to 85 across the 30 departments. The histogram shows a main concentration of ratings around the mid-60s, with a tail extending toward lower ratings. All three predictors show positive associations with overall workplace rating. Complaint handling has the clearest approximately linear relationship, whereas learning opportunities and performance-based raises show more scatter around their fitted lines. There is no obvious strong curvature in these plots. Thus, linear relationships is a reasonable starting point. Some departments lie far away from the fitted lines, such as one with a learning score near 58 and an overall rating of 40. During regression diagnostics, we would need to pay closer attention to these observations. The positive associations are consistent with the expectation that more favorable views of complaint handling, learning opportunities, and performance-based raises accompany higher overall workplace ratings. Importantly, these department-level associations do not establish causation. ## Model Specification
